title: The fragmentation of resistance in Afghanistan
gist: Five years after the Taliban's return to power, Afghanistan's armed opposition is a fragmented collection of competing fronts (AFF, NRF, Afghanistan United Front and smaller groups) with no common command, coherent political program, or foreign patron — a disunity the author argues is currently the Taliban's best protection, though a future influx of arms or a shift toward territorial control could turn today's fragmentation into a dangerous free-for-all among rival commanders.

insights.claim: Afghanistan does not have a unified armed resistance so much as a collection of armed groups operating separately under ambitious leaders with different constituencies, patrons and political ambitions, mirrored by a similarly fragmented opposition abroad with no common command, coherent political program, or agreement on who should govern if Taliban rule ends.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Central framework for assessing Afghan political risk: treat 'the resistance' as multiple uncoordinated actors, not a unified opposition bloc, when forecasting Taliban regime stability.
insights.quote: Afghanistan does not have an armed resistance so much as a collection of armed groups, operating separately under ambitious leaders with different constituencies, patrons and political ambitions.
insights.locator: Perhaps. But it is getting hard to see the wood for the trees

insights.claim: This disunity among the Taliban's opponents is currently helping keep the Taliban secure, since no resistance movement controls territory and the recent uptick in attacks falls far short of a sustained national insurgency.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Direct causal claim: Taliban regime stability today rests significantly on opposition fragmentation rather than Taliban strength alone — a fragile equilibrium that could shift quickly if the fronts unify or gain a patron.
insights.quote: That disunity is helping keep the Taliban secure.
insights.locator: That fragmentation mirrors the Afghan opposition abroad

insights.claim: A former Afghan general with men operating inside the country told the author there are a dozen resistance fronts, which makes coordination difficult, and voiced fear that the groups will start fighting each other.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A first-hand source quantifying the fragmentation (roughly a dozen fronts) and flagging intra-opposition conflict as a live risk, relevant to modeling worst-case Afghan instability scenarios beyond just Taliban-vs-opposition conflict.
insights.quote: There are a dozen fronts, which makes things difficult to coordinate between them... My fear is they will start fighting each other.
insights.locator: a former Afghan general with men operating inside the country told me

insights.claim: Numbers and geographic proliferation of armed groups should not be misconstrued as military strength or cohesion; small, scattered attacks may expose weaknesses in Taliban control but also reveal to the Taliban where those weaknesses lie, allowing the regime to reinforce local security before threats become serious.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Counterintuitive risk-assessment point: more visible resistance activity can paradoxically strengthen the regime by revealing threat locations for pre-emptive suppression, rather than weakening it.
insights.quote: Numbers and geographic proliferation should not be misconstrued as military strength or cohesion.
insights.locator: A plethora of smaller groups are popping up

themes.theme: The major fronts and their leaders

insights.claim: The Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF), led by General Yasin Zia — a former Afghan Army chief, deputy defence minister, deputy head of the national intelligence agency and governor of Takhar province — has developed a detailed political manifesto for a post-Taliban state and has concentrated recent activity in the north and northeast, including sustained clashes around Zebak district in Badakhshan in July that lasted several days, unusual for a resistance campaign typically characterised by hit-and-run attacks.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: AFF stands out among resistance groups for having both a coherent political plan and unusually sustained combat activity — the front most worth tracking as a potential organizing pole if fragmentation later resolves.

insights.claim: The National Resistance Front (NRF), led by Ahmad Massoud (son of famed anti-Soviet commander Ahmad Shah Massoud), is the best-known armed opposition movement, drawing heavily on the political symbolism and networks of the old Northern Alliance, and operates separately from the AFF.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: NRF's name-recognition and historical legitimacy make it the most internationally visible resistance brand, but its lack of coordination with AFF underscores the article's fragmentation thesis.
insights.locator: The National Resistance Front of Ahmad Massoud

insights.claim: Sami Sadat, the former commander of Afghanistan's special forces, leads the Afghanistan United Front from exile, presenting himself as a national leader-in-waiting who promises to 'take back Afghanistan' and restore constitutional government, but his organisation does not provide a bridge between the disparate armed fronts.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A third major but separate leadership claimant, reinforcing that Afghanistan's opposition has at least three competing would-be national leaders with no unifying mechanism among them.

themes.theme: No foreign patron, unlike the 1980s mujahideen

insights.claim: Unlike the anti-Soviet mujahideen, who had Pakistan, the United States, Saudi Arabia and other states supplying money and weapons, today's anti-Taliban groups have sympathisers abroad but no apparent pipeline of sustained foreign military or financial support, though this could change as relations between the Taliban and its former patron Islamabad continue to deteriorate.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Absence of a foreign patron is a key structural constraint keeping the resistance weak and fragmented; a deteriorating Taliban-Pakistan relationship is the clearest potential trigger to watch for a shift toward external funding of Afghan opposition groups.
insights.quote: There is no obvious external patron capable of uniting these groups into a cohesive anti-Taliban fighting force.
insights.locator: There is no obvious external patron

insights.claim: If foreign money and weapons did begin flowing to Afghan resistance groups, it would immediately raise the destabilising question of who among the competing fronts gets them, since the men leading these fronts are not just military commanders but prospective political leaders with their own ideas about how the country should be ruled.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Flags a specific future risk scenario: any external arms/funding influx to Afghan resistance groups is likely to sharpen inter-group rivalry rather than simply strengthen anti-Taliban capability, given the absence of a unifying command structure.
insights.locator: This could change, as could the military balance

insights.claim: The Taliban originally emerged from a protracted civil war fought by powerful, rival warlords each convinced he should lead the country, during which an estimated 25,000 people were killed in Kabul alone as factions fired rockets and artillery across frontlines sometimes separated by the width of a street.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A concrete historical casualty figure (25,000 killed in Kabul) that grounds the author's warning that today's leadership rivalry among resistance commanders echoes the exact dynamic that produced the Taliban's original rise to power.
insights.locator: Afghanistan has seen this movie before

insights.claim: Today's armed opposition groups lack the firepower and manpower of the 1990s warlords, many of whom now live in Europe or the United States with retinues and dreams of a triumphal return.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Suggests today's resistance, while fragmented like the 1990s factions, is currently much weaker militarily — implying any near-term Taliban collapse scenario is less likely than the disorder-risk-if-it-does-happen scenario.
insights.locator: Today's armed groups lack the firepower

insights.claim: The author concludes that if the divisions among the Taliban's enemies change, Afghanistan's resistance fronts might find that overthrowing their common enemy was only the beginning, with the hardest part being deciding who among them should inherit the state.
insights.speaker: Lynne O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Frames the highest-risk future scenario for Afghanistan not as continued Taliban rule but as a post-Taliban succession crisis among rival resistance leaders — the article's core forward-looking warning.
insights.quote: The hardest part might be deciding who among them should inherit the state.
